hints: Look carefully at Fig. 2.1 - where are the chromosomes positioned in the cell and what structures are attached to their centromeres?
walkthrough:
Read the Picture Like a Snapshot of Mitosis**
You are seeing chromosomes lined up in a single row across the middle of the cell, the equator. Spindle fibres from opposite poles are attached to the centromere of each chromosome. That lining-up stage is the hallmark of metaphase.

Rule Out the Neighbours**
It is not prophase because the nuclear envelope has broken down and chromosomes are already attached to the spindle, not just condensing. It is not anaphase because sister chromatids have not yet separated and moved to poles.

hints: Count the double-chromatid chromosomes lined up in Fig. 2.1, then think about what happens to each pair of sister chromatids when anaphase pulls them apart.
Think about what identical means for the two new nuclei - how many single chromatids and what mixture of sizes or shades must each nucleus receive?
walkthrough:
Count What You Start With**
Fig. 2.1 shows 4 chromosomes on the metaphase plate, each made of two sister chromatids. Notice there are two types: two longer/darker and two shorter/lighter. That is the diploid set.

Follow Chromatids Through Anaphase**
In anaphase each centromere splits and one sister chromatid from every chromosome is pulled to each pole. So each pole gets 4 single-chromatid chromosomes, not 4 double ones. A common slip is to draw X-shapes again - after separation they are V or rod shapes with one chromatid only.

Make the Two Nuclei Identical**
Inside each dotted nuclear envelope in Fig. 2.2 draw the same set: 4 single chromatids comprising two long/dark and two short/light. Both top and bottom cells must match each other and match the original types.
Final answer: Draw in each forming nucleus (inside dotted line): 4 single-chromatid daughter chromosomes, shown as two pairs e.g. two long/dark and two short/light, identical in both cells.

hints: Remember that DNA polymerase cannot fully copy the very tip of a linear chromosome, so think about what kind of DNA it would be safest to lose from the end.
walkthrough:
Why Chromosome Ends Are a Problem**
Linear chromosomes shorten a little with each round of DNA replication because the lagging strand cannot be completed right to the tip. Without a buffer, useful coding DNA would be cut off.

Telomeres as Disposable Buffers**
Telomeres are repeated non-coding DNA sequences at the ends. They are sacrificed instead, so no genes or genetic information are lost. They also stop chromosome ends sticking together by fusion.
Final answer: Prevent loss of genes / genetic information during DNA replication.

hints: Start from the two special properties of stem cells - what can they do in terms of dividing and in terms of changing into other cell types?
Think about why healthy cells are grown in the laboratory first before being put back - what does mitosis allow you to achieve in numbers?
Link the return of cells to what radiation has just done to the marrow - what normal cell population needs to be rebuilt and by what process?
walkthrough:
Expand Healthy Cells Outside the Body**
Stem cells can divide by mitosis, so the isolated healthy stem cells can be multiplied in the laboratory to give large numbers for transplant. This gives enough cells to restart the marrow.

Keep Them Flexible Until Needed**
Stem cells are undifferentiated or unspecialised, meaning they have not yet committed to one job. That is why they can be stored and grown without losing potential.

Rebuild Blood After Radiation**
Radiation wipes out cancerous and normal marrow stem cells. When the lab-grown healthy stem cells are returned, they can differentiate or specialise into the different blood cell types. By continued mitosis plus differentiation they re-populate the marrow and bring blood cells back to normal levels.

Final answer: Stem cells grown in the lab divide by mitosis to increase numbers; stem cells are undifferentiated / unspecialised; after return they differentiate / specialise into different blood cell types to repopulate / replace blood cells to normal levels.
